title: Implicit Inversion turns CLIP into a Decoder
claim: A decoder-free approach can synthesize diverse, high-quality samples from simple scene prompts and complex captions alone.
layout: 2 rows by 6 columns gallery, captions beneath each image
description: A 2×6 grid of generated images with a short text prompt under each one. The top row shows generic scene prompts: Mt Pinatubo eruption, Tibetan monastery on a cliff, Prague castle, Machu Picchu shrouded in mist, Grand Canyon at sunset, and Photo of Uluru. These are dramatic, saturated landscapes with a painterly, slightly surreal texture. The bottom row shows longer MS-COCO-style captions, including a group of people sitting around a table, a retro 1969s living room, a pastry store with cupcakes, oranges stacked in a bowl, a man standing near a bed, and a kitchen with cabinets. These look like oil paintings with muted, warm tones. The captions use a monospace typewriter font on a white background. There are no arrows, modules, or diagrams. The eye goes first to the vivid top-row landscapes.
caption: Decoder-free text-to-image synthesis. CLIP$^{-1}$ inverts CLIP's image encoder using implicit neural representations, enabling text-to-image synthesis without any fine-tuning or dedicated generative decoder. All samples are generated with CLIP ViT-B/32 [ref], with top rows showing generic scene prompts and bottom rows illustrating complex captions from MS-COCO [ref].
abstract: CLIP is a discriminative model trained to align images and text in a shared embedding space. Due to its multimodal structure, it serves as the backbone of many generative pipelines, where a decoder is trained to map from the shared space back to images. In this work, we show that image synthesis is nevertheless possible using CLIP alone -- without any decoder, training, or fine-tuning. Our approach optimizes a frequency-aware implicit neural representation that encourages coarse-to-fine generation by stratifying frequencies across network layers. To stabilize this inverse mapping, we introduce adversarially robust initialization, a lightweight Orthogonal Procrustes projection to align local text and image embeddings, and a blending loss that anchors outputs to natural image statistics. Without altering CLIP's weights, this framework unlocks capabilities such as text-to-image generation, style transfer, and image reconstruction. These findings suggest that discriminative models may hold untapped generative potential, hidden in plain sight.
